The thorium point is slightly wrong. Thorium 232 can absorb a neutron then beta decay into Uranium 233, which can be chemically separated, especially with liquid fuels. The military successfully tested a U233 bomb. 

Power reactors are actually not that good at making bomb material. You can make a bomb out of U235, but its abundance is .7% of all uranium isotope, and you need a >80% concentration of U235 for that. About 99% of naturally occurring Uranium is U238, which cannot undergo a chain reaction. What you can do is have it absorb a neutron then beta decay into Neptunium 239 then into Plutonium 239. That isotope of plutonium is ideal, and a high neutron environment is in a reactor.  
But there is good news for power reactors. If Pu 239 absorbs a neutron it becomes Pu240, which is too radioactive to use in a bomb. The isotope accumulation rates are fairly well known, and 90 days of operation is the benchmark where Pu 240 build up starts. Thus people trying to build a plutonium bomb with a power reactor would have to stop it every 3 months to remove the fuel rods, which is very obvious to regulators.
